prompt: Two items in the `orders` container are both called `o-1001`. How can that be?
hint: Look at their `customerId`.

choices.text: An `id` is unique only within one partition key value
choices.why: Right: identity is the pair.

choices.text: The emulator does not check `id`s, and Azure would refuse the second
choices.why: The emulator refused a true duplicate with 409.

choices.text: `upsert_item` renamed the second one silently
choices.why: Both kept their `id`; they differ in customer.

choices.text: `id`s are unique per database, and these are in two
choices.why: One database, one container.

prompt: What does a point read, `read_item`, need to find an order?
hint: Both halves of the identity.

choices.text: The `id` alone
choices.why: Two items can share it.

choices.text: The `_rid` the service assigned
choices.why: That is internal; the read in `model.py` used `id` and key.

choices.text: A query with `enable_cross_partition_query`
choices.why: That is a query, not a point read.

choices.text: The `id` together with the partition key value
choices.why: Right.

prompt: What HTTP status did the emulator answer for an item of 2.1 MB?
hint: Payload Too Large.

prompt: Quitanda wants each order to keep a list of every event in its life, appended forever. What will happen?
hint: An item has a ceiling.

choices.text: An order eventually passes 2 MB and its next write fails
choices.why: Right: an unbounded list inside one item is a design that fails on a write.

choices.text: Cosmos DB moves the list to a second item when it is full
choices.why: Nothing splits an item for you.

choices.text: The logical partition reaches 20 GB on the first year
choices.why: One order's events are far from 20 GB; the item limit comes first.

choices.text: Nothing; items have no size limit
choices.why: The emulator refused 2.1 MB with 413.

prompt: What is a logical partition?
hint: You choose it by choosing the key.

choices.text: A piece of Azure's storage and compute
choices.why: That is a physical partition.

choices.text: A range of the hash, split as the container grows
choices.why: A logical partition is never split.

choices.text: Every item that shares one value of the partition key
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: A container inside a database
choices.why: A container holds many logical partitions.

prompt: At most how many GB can one logical partition hold, according to the documentation?
hint: It is never split, so it has a hard limit.

prompt: A container has 40,000 RU/s over four physical partitions. Half of all writes carry one key value. How many RU/s can those writes use at most?
hint: One value lives in one physical partition, and the throughput is shared evenly.

prompt: A container throttles every evening while its average use is under a third of what it pays for. What is the likeliest cause?
hint: Average across partitions, limits per partition.

choices.text: Too little throughput, bought for the average
choices.why: The average says there is spare throughput; it is in the wrong place.

choices.text: The items are larger than 2 MB
choices.why: That fails writes with 413, not throttling.

choices.text: Too many physical partitions, each with too little to do
choices.why: Idle partitions do not throttle the busy one; the busy one's share does.

choices.text: A hot partition
choices.why: Right: one key value takes the evening's load.

prompt: `reads.py` showed 1 RU for every read. What does that tell you about Azure's prices?
hint: Lesson 1 met this number.

choices.text: That the three reads cost the same on Azure
choices.why: On Azure they differ; the emulator's 1 is a placeholder.

choices.text: That queries are free below a thousand items
choices.why: Nothing here measured a price.

choices.text: Nothing: the emulator charges 1 for everything
choices.why: Right; lesson 13 teaches the real units from the documentation.

choices.text: That a point read costs the same as writing an item
choices.why: No write was measured.

prompt: Why did the cross-partition query take one request here, when on Azure it would take more?
hint: Read the last line of the output.

choices.text: The library batched the partitions into one request
choices.why: It sends one per partition; there was one.

choices.text: The emulator has a single physical partition
choices.why: Right: `feed ranges in the container: 1`.

choices.text: `enable_cross_partition_query` collapses the fan-out
choices.why: It only allows the query to be sent.

choices.text: The query matched only 40 items
choices.why: The fan-out follows the partitions, not the result size.

prompt: On Azure, order these reads of the same data from cheapest to dearest.
hint: The more the engine has to do and visit, the dearer.
items: A point read by `id` and key
A query naming the key's value
A query on another field, across partitions

prompt: The Python library refuses to send a query that visits every partition unless the call sets the option ___ to `True`.
hint: Four words joined by underscores, as `reads.py` wrote it.

prompt: `/placedDate` had 365 values of 274 orders each. Why is it still a bad key for orders?
hint: Look at the hot hour column.

choices.text: Each evening's writes all carry today's date
choices.why: Right: 100% of the evening on one value.

choices.text: Its partitions pass 20 GB within the year
choices.why: 274 orders a day is tiny.

choices.text: Dates cannot be partition keys in Cosmos DB
choices.why: Any string path can be.

choices.text: Too many values, which wastes physical partitions
choices.why: 365 values is few, not many.

prompt: Besides its three values, what makes `/status` wrong as a partition key in a way the table cannot show?
hint: What happens to an order between `paid` and `delivered`?

choices.text: Status strings are too short to hash well
choices.why: Hashing does not care about length.

choices.text: Queries by status are refused on Cosmos DB
choices.why: They are allowed; across partitions if status is not the key.

choices.text: It changes over an order's life, and moving an item to another key means deleting and rewriting it
choices.why: Right: a delete and a new write every time.

choices.text: Status is not unique, and a key has to be
choices.why: The key is meant to repeat; the `id` is what is unique within it.

prompt: At about 1 KB an order, roughly how many million orders fill one logical partition's 20 GB? Use 1 GB = 1,000,000 KB.
hint: Twenty gigabytes of kilobytes.

prompt: `rekey.py` asked the emulator to change the partition key to `/placedDate`. What happened?
hint: Compare `before` and `after`.

choices.text: The emulator refused it with an error
choices.why: It returned without an error.

choices.text: The key changed, and the items were rehashed
choices.why: `after` still said `/customerId`.

choices.text: It answered success and kept `/customerId`
choices.why: Right: a success that did nothing.

choices.text: A new container was created beside the old one
choices.why: No container was created; the old one is unchanged.

prompt: With the key `/customerId` then `/orderMonth`, what does a point read have to name?
hint: `hier.py` said it.

choices.text: The `id` and the customer
choices.why: That is a prefix, enough for a query and not for a point read.

choices.text: The `id`, the customer and the month
choices.why: Right: every level.

choices.text: The month alone, since it is the deepest level
choices.why: A level cannot be named without those above it.

choices.text: The `id` alone, since the key is hierarchical
choices.why: The hierarchy adds to what a read must name.

prompt: How many levels can a hierarchical partition key have at most?
hint: The section's first sentence.

prompt: When is a hierarchical key worth its cost over a plain `/customerId`?
hint: What problem does the second level solve?

choices.text: When one customer outgrows a logical partition
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Whenever a container has more than one kind of item
choices.why: That is a design question, not one of size.

choices.text: When queries need to sort by month
choices.why: Sorting is a query's `ORDER BY`, not a key.

choices.text: When the emulator has a single physical partition
choices.why: The emulator's shape says nothing about Azure's need.

prompt: Quitanda's app also needs a screen listing every order placed in the last hour, for the warehouse. With `/customerId` as the key, what does that screen cost?
hint: Which partitions hold the last hour's orders?

choices.text: A query in one partition, since the hour is recent
choices.why: Recent orders are spread over thousands of customers.

choices.text: A point read per order
choices.why: The screen does not know the `id`s in advance.

choices.text: Nothing extra: Cosmos DB indexes the date
choices.why: An index helps inside each partition; the query still visits every one.

choices.text: A cross-partition query, dearer as the container splits
choices.why: Right; a second, rarer question pays for the key chosen for the first.
